newsitem.title: JAPAN: China and HK speak with one voice at ADB.
newsitem.headline: China and HK speak with one voice at ADB.

text.p: Beijing and Hong Kong economic officials have gone on a charm offensive at the Asian Development Bank (ADB) meeting to assure the world of no financial shocks when the British colony returns to China.

While political rows keep breaking out over the handover, China's central bank governor Dai Xiang and Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief Joseph Yam have spoken with one voice in this southern city where the ADB's annual meeting opened on Sunday.
Their message: No interference by China that would threaten Hong Kong's role as a world financial centre.

"We will work to ensure that Hong Kong will remain as an international (financial) centre after its return," Dai, governor of the People's Bank of China, told Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka in a meeting on Saturday night.
Japanese officials, who briefed reporters on the meeting, said Dai repeatedly gave the assurance during the talks.
Japan is one of the largest investors in Hong Kong and Chinese officials are keen not to see a flight of capital when Hong Kong returns to China on July 1.
"Dai repeatedly stressed that the 'one nation, two systems' policy was for financial matters as well as politics," a Japanese official said.
Yam also did his bit to assure Asian financial policy makers and businessmen at the meeting that come July 1 there would be no surprises.
"There is no meaningful conversion to talk about in terms of (post-handover) policy," Yam told a business seminar on Saturday.
He said there were no signs of China changing its pledge to allow Hong Kong to hold a currency and monetary system of its own that would be administered by an authority separate from the China.
He also said the Hong Kong dollar will remain pegged to the U.S. dollar after the handover, and that China will have no influence over Hong Kong's $60 to $70 billion of foreign currency reserves.
He specifically ruled out the reserves being used to invest in China's state-run enterprises, some of which are in poor financial shape.
"We are not 100 percent sure, we are 600 percent sure," Yam said.
But in a nod to cooperation with Beijing, Yam said the two needed to work together for Hong Kong's growth.

"Of course there is a need for very close cooperation between the two monetary authorities and the two monetary systems, in order to continue to sustain economic prosperity and stability in Hong Kong and for Hong Kong to continue to develop as an international financial centre," Yam said.
